name: Monte Verde (MV-II)
hook: A peat-sealed campsite in southern Chile that broke Clovis-first; its age was challenged again in 2026.
claim: Tom Dillehay's team reported that Monte Verde II, a campsite with wooden structures, hearths, tools, plant foods and gomphothere remains sealed under peat, was occupied about 13,000 radiocarbon years ago, before the accepted Clovis-first limit.

claimed_age.label: ~13,000 14C yr BP; revised ~12,500 (~14,500 cal BP)
claimed_age.basis: First reports (1982-88): ~13,000 14C yr BP (S3); the 1997 panel accepted ~12,500 (S6). bp_min/bp_max are the team's current calibrated MV-II range (S12), not a calibration of 13,000.

accepted_age.label: ~14,500 cal BP (majority view; disputed since 2026)
accepted_age.basis: Calibrated 14C on occupation materials (S12); hearth seaweed 14,220-13,980 cal BP (S9). Surovell et al. (S13) argue MV-II is no older than the mid-Holocene (8,200-4,200 BP).

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Clovis-first: no human entry into the Americas before ~13,000 cal BP; earlier claims were rejected.

unambiguous_signal.note: Wooden structures, knotted reeds and a few bifaces, but most stone tools were simple edge-trimmed pebbles (S10); Lynch warned that natural processes can mimic hearths and tools.

documented_context.note: A 1986 report called MV-II a small, well-preserved residential settlement (S2); later reports describe a thin layer sealed by peat (S12). Recording errors surfaced later (S11, S21).

multiple_dating_methods.note: Radiocarbon only (wood, bone, charcoal). Later luminescence dates came from other parts of the site (S10) and nearby creek exposures (S13), not MV-II.

multiple_labs.note: Lab names and assay years for the 1982-88 dates were not confirmed; S12 says only that dates came from different labs over four decades.

professional_recovery.note: University team led by Dillehay with a large interdisciplinary group of specialists.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Short reports in 1982, 1986 and 1988 (S1, S2, S3); the full site volumes came in 1989 and 1997 (S12).

material_accessible.note: No source found on critics' access in the 1980s; outside specialists examined the collections and site in 1997.

independent_teams.note: Many specialists, all within Dillehay's project. Outside checks came later (1997 panel, S6; Taylor's lab, S20); S13 calls itself the first independent investigation.

proponent_stake.note: None documented in the sources reviewed (an absence of evidence, not proof); results went to scholarly journals (S2, S3).

objections.text: With the Clovis horizon ever better defined and earlier claims failing, a glacial-age (pre-Clovis) occupation of South America was improbable.
objections.outcome_note: A 2019 review: genetics puts people south of the ice sheets between ~17.5 and ~14.6 ka, and sites show them in multiple places at ~15.5-14 ka (S22). Surovell et al. (2026) argue for later arrival.

objections.text: Archaeologists should depend more on unambiguous and replicated cases before accepting glacial-age occupation.
objections.outcome_note: Outside checks came from the 1997 panel (S6) and Taylor's lab (S8); the first independent field dating study came only in 2026 (S13, S16) and is itself untested.

objections.text: Natural processes can mimic informal hearths and simple stone tools; the 'hand of humans' at the site was not established.
objections.outcome_note: The 1997 panel judged MV-II archaeological (S6); the 2026 challengers also call it an 'archaeological component' (S13). If its dated wood was redeposited, whether those pieces were worked is open again.

objections.text: The artifacts' association with the dated Pleistocene layer was unproven; mixture or secondary deposition could explain it.
objections.outcome_note: Accepted by the 1997 panel (S6), and direct hearth-seaweed dates fit (S9). The same secondary-deposition mechanism was re-argued in 2026 (S13) and has no outside test yet.

objections.text: Published provenience records were inconsistent and key artifacts poorly documented, so their association with the dated surface was not demonstrated.
objections.outcome_note: Errors in the 1997 volume led to a 2002 errata booklet (S11), and a 1989 date was misattributed to MV-II (corrected 2023, S21). The team says all finds are documented; Fiedel renewed the charge in 2022.

objections.text: Two dates on one gomphothere bone disagreed by over 5,000 years, and a postulated local 14C reservoir effect could have made the site's dates too old.
objections.raised_by: R. E. Taylor et al. (tested the concerns)
objections.outcome_note: No offset in modern site plants (S20), though Pleistocene offsets cannot be measured directly; AMS redates of the bone gave 12,460 ± 30 BP (S8); S12 traces the outlier to one lab.

objections.text: Ash dated ~11,000 years lies stratigraphically below the archaeological component, and the Pleistocene-dated wood was redeposited, so MV-II is no older than the mid-Holocene (8,200-4,200 BP).
objections.outcome_note: Disputed by geoarchaeologists outside the site team (tephra not Lepué; correlation unproven; S15, S17), by the site team and by Meltzer et al. Surovell remains confident (S18). No outside test yet.

status_note: Re-contested since 2026 (S13). Kept vindicated: the challengers' own 14C dates (13,400-16,500 yr) match earlier ones (S14), and their key evidence, a tephra link, is disputed on its geochemistry (S15, S17) and untested by an outside lab.
what_settled_it: In January 1997 a group of Paleoindian specialists examined the collections and visited the site, and agreed MV-II was archaeological and ~12,500 radiocarbon years old. Later direct dates on hearth seaweed (S9) and outside-lab redating of a gomphothere bone (S8) agreed.

timeline.event: The site is discovered in southern Chile.
First radiocarbon report puts the MV-II occupation at about 13,000 radiocarbon years.
A Nature report adds dates near 33,000 radiocarbon years for a possible older layer (MV-I).
Lynch's review questions the finds' human origin and Pleistocene association, and asks for replicated cases.
Paleoindian specialists examine the collections and site and agree MV-II is archaeological and ~12,500 years old.
Fiedel argues the published provenience records cannot demonstrate association.
Taylor et al. find no local 14C reservoir offset in modern plants at the site.
Outside-lab AMS redating of a discordant gomphothere bone gives 12,460 ± 30 radiocarbon years.
Seaweed from MV-II hearths is directly dated to 14,220-13,980 cal BP.
Forty-three dates on the sealing peat, from a section ~50 m north of MV-II, place its base near 14,500-14,600 cal BP.
Surovell et al. argue MV-II is no older than the mid-Holocene (8,200-4,200 BP), citing an underlying tephra and redeposited wood.
Replies in Science eLetters and PaleoAmerica (Waters et al., site team, Meltzer et al.) reject it; Surovell remains confident.

decisive_tests.test: At a lab outside both teams, AMS-date blind splits of identified short-lived plants (reed cordage, food plants) and seaweed from archived MV-II collections; apply a local marine reservoir correction to seaweed.
decisive_tests.would_show: Pleistocene ages on short-lived remains rule out redeposited old wood; mid-Holocene ages support Surovell et al. (Charcoal can only show a young age.) Needs sampling permits.

decisive_tests.test: Blind glass-chemistry fingerprinting, at a lab outside both teams, of the ash Surovell et al. call Lepué Tephra, against reference Lepué samples and any ash in the site team's section ~50 m north of MV-II.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the ash is the ~11,000-year Lepué Tephra and whether it lies below MV-II-equivalent peat, the core of the mid-Holocene argument.

decisive_tests.test: Wood and bone taphonomy (abrasion, rounding, decay) on archived MV-II material, plus micromorphology of any archived MV-II sediment, compared with wood the creek deposits today.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether MV-II wood and bone were carried in by water or used in place.

decisive_tests.test: Permitted joint fieldwork, logged by both teams and an outside geologist, tracing the peat and ash beds continuously from Surovell et al.'s creek exposures to the site team's section ~50 m north of MV-II.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the dated creek exposures and the site-team section are the same beds; MV-II itself was destroyed decades ago, so the correlation must be traced nearby.

falsifier: An outside lab confirming the ~11,000-year Lepué Tephra beneath MV-II-equivalent peat (e.g. in the section ~50 m north) would move this record to 'open'; mid-Holocene AMS ages on short-lived plant remains from archived MV-II collections would point to 'refuted'.

sources.citation: Dillehay TD, Collins MB. 1988. Early cultural evidence from Monte Verde in Chile. Nature 332(6160): 150-152.

sources.note: Read: findspots of key artifacts inadequately documented; site 'should not be construed as conclusive proof', i.e. unproven, not refuted.

sources.note: Full text read: MV-II ~14,500 cal BP; MV-I (~33,000 BP) too meager to verify; possible horizons ~18,500-14,500 cal BP; luminescence dates are from units south of the creek, not MV-II.

sources.citation: Dillehay TD, Pino M, Ocampo C, Adovasio J, Collins MB, Saavedra J, Rossen J, Pollock D. 2022. Correcting Fiedel, Once Again: Monte Verde and the Peopling of South America. Radiocarbon 64(4): 899-904.
sources.note: Full text read: 1997 volume errors fixed by a 2002 errata booklet; 70+ specialists; MV-II a sealed single component.

sources.note: Full text read: 43 new AMS dates from a section ~50 m north of MV-II; MV-II 14,200-14,900 cal BP; bone outlier from one lab, Taylor's redating; Clovis-first entry 'no earlier than c. 13 000 cal BP'.

sources.citation: Surovell TA, Méndez C, García J-L, Lüthgens C, Thompson JM, Latorre C. 2026. A mid-Holocene age for Monte Verde challenges the timeline of human colonization of South America. Science 391(6791): 1283-1288.
sources.note: Abstract read: 'first independent investigation' in ~50 years; 14C and luminescence dates on alluvial exposures and an 11,000-yr tephra below the component: MV-II no older than 8,200-4,200 BP.

sources.citation: Killgrove K. 2026. Monte Verde, one of the earliest Indigenous sites in South America, is much younger than thought, study claims. Live Science, 19 March 2026.
sources.note: Read: MV-II destroyed >30 years ago by logging and flooding; Surovell's team sampled nearby; new dates 13,400-16,500 yr 'in line with previous studies'; lists a human footprint.

sources.citation: Waters MR, Halligan JJ, Mandel RD, Holcomb JA, Davis LG, Holliday VT; Dillehay TD, Pino M, Lara L, et al.; Meltzer DJ, Moreno-Mayar JV, et al. 2026. Three eLetters responding to Surovell et al. (2026), Science, 4-5 May 2026. Compiled PDF, Center for the Study of the First Americans, Texas A&M University.
sources.note: Read: screened eLetters, not peer-reviewed. Geology (Waters et al.: tephra 'not the Lepué Tephra'), site evidence (Dillehay et al.) and genetics (Meltzer et al.) reject the mid-Holocene age.

sources.citation: Tune JW, Miller DS. 2026. Replication as a Virtue: What the Monte Verde Debate Tells Us About Archaeological Science. PaleoAmerica 12(1): 5-9.
sources.note: Abstract read: calls Surovell et al. the first truly independent geochronological study of MV-II; long lack of replication was structural. Takes no side on the age.

sources.citation: Waters MR, Halligan JJ, Mandel RD, Holcomb JA, Davis LG, Holliday VT. 2026. Evaluation of the Geoarchaeological Study that Proposes a Middle Holocene Age for Monte Verde II, Chile. PaleoAmerica: 1-3.
sources.note: Abstract read: the mid-Holocene geology and secondary-context scenarios are 'flawed and inadequate'; decades of evidence support ~14.4 ka for MV-II.

sources.citation: Dunham W. 2026. Researchers defend older age of key archaeological site in Chile. Reuters, 31 August 2026.
sources.note: Read (Reuters via Yahoo): two groups defend the older age in PaleoAmerica; Surovell 'remains confident' and calls for independent study.

sources.citation: Taylor RE, Haynes CV, Kirner DL, Southon JR. 1999. Radiocarbon Analyses of Modern Organics at Monte Verde, Chile: No Evidence for a Local Reservoir Effect. American Antiquity 64(3): 455-460.
sources.note: Abstract read: modern plants at the site show no 14C offset, so no support for a postulated reservoir effect; late-Pleistocene offsets cannot be measured directly.

sources.citation: Dillehay TD. 2023. Correction for a Monte Verde II Radiocarbon Date. PaleoAmerica 9(2): 165-166.
sources.note: Abstract read: a La Moderna (Argentina) date was published in 1989 as an MV-II assay in error; corrected here.

sources.citation: Waters MR. 2019. Late Pleistocene exploration and settlement of the Americas by modern humans. Science 365(6449).
sources.note: Abstract read: genetics puts people south of the ice sheets ~17.5-14.6 ka; sites in North and South America ~15.5-14 ka. The author also leads the 2026 rebuttal (S17).

confidence_note: Paywalled sources read as abstracts; full texts of S13 and S17 not read, the eLetters (S15) were. The 2026 re-contest is live, and an outside test could change the status.
corrections: Brief: 'Pre-Clovis occupation at ~14,500 years'. First reports (1982-88) gave ~13,000 14C yr BP (S3); the 1997 panel accepted ~12,500 14C yr BP (S6), which calibrates to ~14,500 cal BP (S12).
Brief: 'dismissed for about twenty years before acceptance'. About 15 years passed from the first dated report (1982, S3) to the 1997 panel (S6); about 20 from the 1976 discovery (S14).
Brief: 'a 1997 site visit by skeptics is often credited with the shift'. The panel also studied the collections, not only the site (S6).

Brief: 'Expected status: vindicated'. That is the majority view, not unanimous: Fiedel (1999, 2022) disputed the provenience records (S7), and Surovell et al. (2026) argue MV-II is no older than 8,200-4,200 BP (S13).

Brief: 'The older Monte Verde I claim (~33,000 years) is separate and still disputed'. The team now calls those levels inconclusive and reports possible, unconfirmed horizons of ~18,500-14,500 cal BP (S10).
Published accounts: a date printed in 1989 as an MV-II assay came from La Moderna, Argentina; the site team corrected it in 2023 (S21).
notes: Covers MV-II only; MV-I (~33,000 14C yr, 1988) was left unresolved by the 1997 panel (S6). MV-II itself was destroyed over 30 years ago by logging and flooding (S14), so both new dating programs used nearby deposits: the site team a section ~50 m north (S12), Surovell's team alluvial exposures (S13, S14). The 2026 eLetters are screened, not peer-reviewed; 1997 panelist Meltzer leads one (S15). Tune and Miller (S16) take no side on the age. Methods count (6): 14C, peat-sealed stratigraphy, artifacts, structures and hearths, plant remains, fauna; the one reported footprint (S14) is not counted separately.

open_issues: Analyst: rerun outcome analyses with MV-II coded 'open' as a sensitivity check. Move it to 'open' if an outside lab confirms Lepué Tephra beneath MV-II-equivalent strata.
S13 full text not read: how it accounts for the direct seaweed dates (S9) and the 2005 bone redating (S8) is unknown.

year_claimed 1982 is the earliest verified dated report (S1, S3); the team says MV-II was first reported in the late 1970s (S12), so time to resolution may be ~18-20 yr, not 15. The unfound 1981 congress paper is dropped.
How much intact MV-II deposit survives is not stated in sources read (S14 reports its destruction); the decisive tests rely on archived collections and nearby sections.
multiple_labs is 'unknown': lab codes and assay years in S1, S3 or the 1989 volume were not read.
Declined: Davis 2026, a reply to Tune and Miller (doi 10.1080/20555563.2026.2670166): no abstract, publisher page 403, and the record is at the 20-source cap.
Declined: Live Science's May 2026 follow-up (S15 gives the eLetters directly). Dropped S5 (1991 reply to Lynch) and S19 (site foundation page) for the 20-source cap; S4 and S14 now cover their uses.
A second 2026 Surovell item ('Surovell et al. 2026a' in S17) was not found by search; it may be a reply worth adding.
